title: Pauri 19, sound: asankh naav

cards: Names for God, or for whatever people mean by the deepest thing, pile up fast. A grandmother uses one word, a friend another, an old hymn a third.

One city street can hold them in several languages, whispered in kitchens and sung behind closed doors. Then there are the places people call holy: rivers, mountains, rooms, a spot under one particular tree.
Pauri 19 starts right there, with names and places, and it says both are beyond counting.

teach.b: Here's the first line of Pauri 19 in the original: asankh naav asankh thaav. Four words, two pairs. Asankh you know: countless.
Naav, said NAAV, with a long a: names. It's a form of naam, the Name, a word at the center of Sikh life. Thaav, THAAV: places.
Hear the rhyme: naav, thaav, the second word landing right on top of the first.
It's the third stanza in a row to lean on asankh. Pauri 17 counted devotions. Pauri 18 counted fools.
Pauri 19 counts names and places, and then, in paraphrase, goes further: countless worlds, beyond reach, beyond reach. Then a twist.
Even to say countless, it says, is to carry a weight on your head. Even the word asankh is too small. Three stanzas built on countless, and Guru Nanak admits that countless isn't big enough either.
The same humility as yesterday, turned on language itself. Tomorrow, where the stanza goes next: to letters and words, and why it doesn't give up on them. Today, the sound.
Asankh naav, asankh thaav. Said slowly, it opens like a wide room. Said quickly, it keeps time like a pulse.
Anyone who recites Japji each morning meets it every day.

how: Pauri 19 is recited in Japji Sahib each morning; its opening line, asankh naav asankh thaav, is the last of the stanzas built on asankh, countless.

o: a pause between two lines of song
names people give to the sacred

games.q: the sound of Pauri 19 — tap the pairs.

s: Pauri 19 says countless names and countless places
Pauri 19 says the word countless is big enough to describe creation
even to say countless is to carry a weight on your head.
naav is a form of naam, the Name
one of the biggest words in Sikh life.

games.q: you've spent three stanzas saying countless. what does Pauri 19 say about the word itself?
o: even saying countless is a weight on your head.
it should be replaced with a number.
games.why: asankh kahahi sir bhaar hoe: even to say countless is a load. the word itself is too small.

practice: Say the first line aloud, asankh naav, asankh thaav: once slowly, feeling the rhyme land, then softer, then almost a whisper. Let it go silent and sit.
If you like, let the words ride quietly on your breath, asankh naav on the in-breath, asankh thaav on the out-breath.

wordCard.voice: Thaav. Places: countless of them, asankh thaav, alongside asankh naav, countless names, and then even countless is called too small a word.

orig.note: Gurmukhi, Japji Pauri 19, line 1: countless names, countless places.

carryVoice: Your line: asankh naav. Countless names, countless places, and even countless too small a word. Until tomorrow.
